title: Gibbs energy and spontaneity
summary: Whether a reaction can happen on its own depends on two things: the [[enthalpy-change|enthalpy change]] and the [[entropy|entropy]] change. The change in [[gibbs-energy|Gibbs energy]], $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, combines them into one number. A negative $\Delta G$ means the change is spontaneous, and $\Delta G$ rises to zero as the reaction reaches equilibrium.

goals.text: Calculate $\Delta G^\ominus$ from $\Delta H^\ominus$, $\Delta S^\ominus$ and $T$, with consistent units, using data from the data booklet.
Explain how $\Delta G$ accounts for the entropy change of both the [[system|system]] and the surroundings.
Use the sign of $\Delta G$ to decide whether a change is spontaneous, and find the crossover temperature where the sign changes.
Describe how $\Delta G$ changes as a reaction approaches equilibrium, and calculate with $\Delta G = \Delta G^\ominus + RT\ln Q$ and $\Delta G^\ominus = -RT\ln K$.

synonyms: delta G equals minus RT ln K

before.prompt: A reaction is carried out at $\pu{45 ^\circ C}$. What is this temperature in [[kelvin|kelvin]], to the nearest kelvin?
before.explain: $T = 45 + 273.15 = 318.15$, so $\pu{318 K}$. Every $T$ in this lesson must be in kelvin. Revise it in {{lesson:1.1}}.

before.prompt: Which change has a positive entropy change, $\Delta S$?
before.hint: Look for the side with more moles of gas.

options.text: a solid breaking down into another solid and a gas
two gases combining to form a solid
a gas condensing to a liquid

before.explain: Making a gas from a solid spreads matter and energy out much more, so entropy rises. The other two changes reduce the amount of gas, so $\Delta S$ is negative. Revise it in {{lesson:4.6}}.

verify.truth: a solid breaking down into another solid and a gas

before.prompt: Methanoic acid can decompose: $\ce{HCOOH(l) -> CO(g) + H2O(l)}$. Use the $S^\ominus$ values in section 13 of the data booklet to calculate $\Delta S^\ominus$, in $\pu{J K-1 mol-1}$. Include the sign.
before.explain: $\Delta S^\ominus = (198 + 70) - 129 = \pu{+139 J K-1 mol-1}$. A gas forms from a liquid, so a positive value makes sense. Revise it in {{lesson:4.6}}.

blocks.text: Two things push a change forward. Releasing heat (a negative $\Delta H$) helps, and so does an increase in entropy (a positive $\Delta S$). In {{lesson:4.6}} you met entropy; now you put the two together.

Often they pull in opposite directions. Ice melting is an [[endothermic-reaction|endothermic]] change, yet it happens on its own above $\pu{0 ^\circ C}$ because the entropy increase wins. Temperature decides which effect matters more.

blocks.statement: $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, where $T$ is the absolute temperature. Under standard conditions it is written $\Delta G^\ominus$.
blocks.plain: One number that weighs the enthalpy change against the entropy change at a given temperature.

blocks.text: The change in [[gibbs-energy|Gibbs energy]] also measures useful energy. When $\Delta G$ is negative, its size is the most energy the reaction can supply as useful work, such as electrical energy from a cell.

This equation is in section 1 of the data booklet. Watch the units: $\Delta H^\ominus$ and $\Delta G^\ominus$ are in $\pu{kJ mol-1}$, but $\Delta S^\ominus$ is in $\pu{J K-1 mol-1}$. Divide $\Delta S^\ominus$ by 1000 before you substitute, and always put $T$ in kelvin.

blocks.question: For $\ce{N2O4(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$, $\Delta H^\ominus = \pu{+57.2 kJ mol-1}$ and $\Delta S^\ominus = \pu{+176 J K-1 mol-1}$. Calculate $\Delta G^\ominus$ at $\pu{298 K}$.
steps: Convert $\Delta S^\ominus$ to kJ: $\pu{+0.176 kJ K-1 mol-1}$.
Substitute: $\Delta G^\ominus = 57.2 - 298 \times 0.176$.
$= 57.2 - 52.448 = \pu{+4.752 kJ mol-1}$, so $\pu{+4.75 kJ mol-1}$ to 3 significant figures.
The positive value means the forward reaction is not spontaneous under standard conditions at $\pu{298 K}$.

blocks.question: Ethanol is made industrially from ethene and steam: $\ce{C2H4(g) + H2O(g) -> C2H5OH(l)}$. Use section 13 of the data booklet to calculate $\Delta G^\ominus$ at $\pu{298 K}$.
steps: $\Delta H^\ominus$ from enthalpies of formation ({{lesson:4.3}}): $-278 - (52 + (-242)) = \pu{-88 kJ mol-1}$.
$\Delta S^\ominus$ from standard entropies: $161 - (220 + 189) = \pu{-248 J K-1 mol-1}$, which is $\pu{-0.248 kJ K-1 mol-1}$.
Sense check: the $\Delta G_\text{f}^\ominus$ column of section 13 gives $-175 - (68 + (-229)) = \pu{-14 kJ mol-1}$, which agrees.

blocks.text: Substituting $\Delta S^\ominus$ in joules next to $\Delta H^\ominus$ in kilojoules gives an answer that is off by thousands. Convert $\Delta S^\ominus$ to $\pu{kJ K-1 mol-1}$ first.

blocks.prompt: A reaction has $\Delta H^\ominus = \pu{-46.0 kJ mol-1}$ and $\Delta S^\ominus = \pu{-99.0 J K-1 mol-1}$. Calculate $\Delta G^\ominus$, in $\pu{kJ mol-1}$, at $\pu{400 K}$. Give 3 significant figures and include the sign.
blocks.hint: $-T\Delta S^\ominus$ is positive here, because $\Delta S^\ominus$ is negative.

blocks.prompt: A reaction has $\Delta H^\ominus = \pu{+31.0 kJ mol-1}$ and $\Delta S^\ominus = \pu{+92.5 J K-1 mol-1}$. What is $\Delta G^\ominus$ at $\pu{360 K}$?
blocks.hint: Put $\Delta S^\ominus$ in kJ before you multiply by $T$.

options.text: $\Delta G^\ominus \approx \pu{-2.30 kJ mol-1}$
$\Delta G^\ominus \approx \pu{+64.3 kJ mol-1}$
$\Delta G^\ominus \approx \pu{+2.30 kJ mol-1}$
$\Delta G^\ominus \approx \pu{-33300 kJ mol-1}$

blocks.explain: $\Delta G^\ominus = 31.0 - 360 \times 0.0925 = 31.0 - 33.3 = \pu{-2.30 kJ mol-1}$. $+64.3$ adds the $T\Delta S$ term, $+2.30$ subtracts the wrong way round, and $-33300$ leaves $\Delta S^\ominus$ in joules.

sections.heading: The sign of $\Delta G$ and spontaneity

blocks.statement: A change that, once started, continues on its own under the stated conditions. At constant temperature and pressure, a change is spontaneous when $\Delta G$ is negative.
blocks.plain: A change that can carry on by itself without a continuous supply of energy from outside.

blocks.statement: At constant temperature and pressure: $\Delta G < 0$, the change is spontaneous; $\Delta G > 0$, it is not spontaneous (but the reverse change is); $\Delta G = 0$, the system is at equilibrium.
blocks.why: $\Delta G$ is $-T$ times the total entropy change of the system and surroundings, and a change happens on its own only if total entropy increases.

blocks.text: Where does the surroundings' entropy come in? A reaction that releases heat warms its surroundings, so their entropy rises by $-\frac{\Delta H}{T}$. Heat taken in lowers it by the same amount. This is the indirect entropy change.

The direct change is $\Delta S$ of the system itself. The total is $\Delta S_\text{total} = \Delta S - \frac{\Delta H}{T}$. Multiply by $-T$ and you get $\Delta H - T\Delta S$, which is $\Delta G$. So a negative $\Delta G$ means total entropy increases.

A [[spontaneous-reaction|spontaneous reaction]] need not be fast. Methane and oxygen have a very negative $\Delta G^\ominus$, but a mixture of them sits unchanged until a spark supplies the activation energy. $\Delta G$ tells you whether a change can happen, not how quickly.

blocks.alt: Graph of standard Gibbs energy change against absolute temperature for four kinds of reaction. Each line starts at the delta H value on the left axis and has gradient minus delta S. Above the zero line is non-spontaneous, below it spontaneous. Delta H negative and delta S positive: always below zero, always spontaneous. Delta H positive and delta S negative: always above zero, never spontaneous. Delta H positive and delta S positive: falls through zero at a crossover temperature, spontaneous above it. Delta H negative and delta S negative: rises through zero at a crossover temperature, spontaneous below it.
blocks.caption: $\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$ is a straight line in $T$. As $T$ rises, the $T\Delta S^\ominus$ term matters more.

blocks.text: Read the four cases from the graph. If $\Delta H$ is negative and $\Delta S$ positive, $\Delta G$ is negative at every temperature. If $\Delta H$ is positive and $\Delta S$ negative, it is never negative.
If $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ have the same sign, there is a crossover temperature where $\Delta G = 0$. Both positive: spontaneous above it. Both negative: spontaneous below it.

To find the crossover, set $\Delta G^\ominus = 0$, so $T = \frac{\Delta H^\ominus}{\Delta S^\ominus}$. This assumes $\Delta H^\ominus$ and $\Delta S^\ominus$ barely change with temperature, which is close enough for IB calculations.

blocks.question: Ammonium nitrate dissolves in water at room temperature, and the solution gets colder. Explain why it dissolves spontaneously.
steps: The solution cools, so the change is endothermic: give the sign of $\Delta H$.
Solid ions spread out through the water: give the sign of $\Delta S$.
Compare the size of $T\Delta S$ with $\Delta H$, then conclude with the sign of $\Delta G$.
blocks.answer: Dissolving is endothermic, so $\Delta H$ is positive, which on its own works against the change. The ions leave the ordered lattice and spread through the solution, so the entropy of the system increases and $\Delta S$ is positive. At room temperature the $T\Delta S$ term is larger than $\Delta H$. So $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ is negative and the dissolving is spontaneous.

verify.truth: endothermic but entropy increases; T delta S exceeds delta H so delta G is negative

blocks.question: For $\ce{ZnCO3(s) -> ZnO(s) + CO2(g)}$, $\Delta H^\ominus = \pu{+68.8 kJ mol-1}$ and $\Delta S^\ominus = \pu{+175 J K-1 mol-1}$. Determine the temperature above which the decomposition is spontaneous.
steps: Both values are positive, so the reaction becomes spontaneous above a crossover temperature.
Set $\Delta G^\ominus = 0$: $T = \frac{\Delta H^\ominus}{\Delta S^\ominus}$.
Use matching units: $T = \frac{68.8}{0.175} = \pu{393.14 K}$.
Above about $\pu{393 K}$ ($\pu{120 ^\circ C}$), $T\Delta S^\ominus$ is larger than $\Delta H^\ominus$, so $\Delta G^\ominus$ is negative.

blocks.text: Reporting a negative temperature. If $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ have opposite signs, $\frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$ is negative and there is no crossover: the reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures or at none.

blocks.prompt: A reaction has $\Delta H^\ominus < 0$ and $\Delta S^\ominus < 0$. Under which conditions is it spontaneous?
blocks.hint: The $-T\Delta S^\ominus$ term is positive, and it grows as $T$ rises.

options.text: only below a certain temperature
only above a certain temperature
at every temperature
at no temperature

blocks.explain: At low $T$ the negative $\Delta H^\ominus$ dominates and $\Delta G^\ominus < 0$. As $T$ rises, $-T\Delta S^\ominus$ grows until $\Delta G^\ominus$ becomes positive.

blocks.prompt: Use section 13 of the data booklet to find the temperature, in K, above which $\ce{H2O(l) -> H2O(g)}$ is spontaneous at $\pu{100 kPa}$. Give 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Find $\Delta H^\ominus$ and $\Delta S^\ominus$ first, then use $T = \frac{\Delta H^\ominus}{\Delta S^\ominus}$ with $\Delta S^\ominus$ in kJ.
blocks.explain: $\Delta H^\ominus = -242 - (-286) = \pu{+44 kJ mol-1}$ and $\Delta S^\ominus = 189 - 70 = \pu{+119 J K-1 mol-1}$. $T = \frac{44}{0.119} \approx \pu{370 K}$, close to the real boiling point of $\pu{373 K}$.

blocks.prompt: A reaction has $\Delta G^\ominus = \pu{-210 kJ mol-1}$ at $\pu{298 K}$, but no change is seen when the reactants are mixed. Which statement is correct?
blocks.hint: What does $\Delta G$ tell you, and what does it not tell you?

options.text: The reaction is spontaneous but very slow at this temperature.
The value must be wrong, because spontaneous reactions are fast.
The reaction is spontaneous only at temperatures above 298 K.

blocks.explain: A negative $\Delta G^\ominus$ says the reaction can happen on its own. It says nothing about rate: a high activation energy can make it too slow to notice.

verify.truth: The reaction is spontaneous but very slow at this temperature.

blocks.text: $\Delta G^\ominus$ is a single value for standard conditions. A real mixture is rarely standard, and its composition changes as it reacts. The value of $\Delta G$ for the actual mixture changes too.

blocks.alt: Graph of the Gibbs energy of a reaction mixture against its composition, from pure reactants on the left to pure products on the right. The curve falls from the left to a minimum about two thirds of the way across, then rises a little to the right end, which is lower than the left end. The minimum is labelled equilibrium, slope zero, delta G equals zero. Left of it the slope is labelled delta G negative, forward reaction spontaneous; right of it, delta G positive, reverse spontaneous. The drop from the left end to the right end is labelled delta G standard.
blocks.caption: $\Delta G$ is the slope of the curve. It is negative on the way down to the minimum and zero at the minimum.

blocks.statement: As a reaction approaches equilibrium, $\Delta G$ becomes less negative and reaches zero at equilibrium. There is then no further net change.
blocks.why: Gibbs energy of the mixture falls to a minimum, and at the minimum nothing can lower it further in either direction.

blocks.text: The data booklet (section 1) links $\Delta G$ to the [[reaction-quotient|reaction quotient]] $Q$, which is the equilibrium expression filled in with the mixture's actual concentrations: $\Delta G = \Delta G^\ominus + RT\ln Q$. Here $R$ is the [[gas-constant|gas constant]], $\pu{8.31 J K-1 mol-1}$ (section 2).

At equilibrium $\Delta G = 0$ and $Q$ equals the [[equilibrium-constant|equilibrium constant]] $K$. Substituting gives $\Delta G^\ominus = -RT\ln K$, also in section 1. Use the natural log, and divide $RT$ by 1000 to get kJ.

The sign of $\Delta G^\ominus$ tells you where equilibrium lies. If $\Delta G^\ominus < 0$, $K > 1$ and products are favoured. If $\Delta G^\ominus > 0$, $K < 1$ and reactants are favoured, though some product still forms. If $\Delta G^\ominus = 0$, $K = 1$.

blocks.question: An esterification has $K = 4.20$ at $\pu{298 K}$. Calculate $\Delta G^\ominus$ for the reaction.
steps: Use $\Delta G^\ominus = -RT\ln K$ with $R = \pu{8.31 J K-1 mol-1}$.
$\Delta G^\ominus = -8.31 \times 298 \times \ln 4.20 = -8.31 \times 298 \times 1.4351 = \pu{-3553.8 J mol-1}$.
Divide by 1000: $\pu{-3.5538 kJ mol-1}$.
$K$ is just above 1, so a small negative $\Delta G^\ominus$ fits: products are slightly favoured.

blocks.question: For $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$, $\Delta G^\ominus = \pu{+4.75 kJ mol-1}$ at $\pu{298 K}$. A mixture at $\pu{298 K}$ has $Q = 0.0100$. Calculate $\Delta G$ for this mixture and deduce which way it reacts.
steps: Use $\Delta G = \Delta G^\ominus + RT\ln Q$, with $RT$ in kJ.
$\Delta G$ is negative, so the forward reaction is spontaneous: more $\ce{NO2}$ forms. As it does, $Q$ rises and $\Delta G$ climbs towards zero.

blocks.text: Using $\log_{10}$ instead of $\ln$, or leaving $RT$ in joules next to $\Delta G^\ominus$ in kilojoules. Both equations need the natural log, and every term in the same units.

blocks.prompt: A reaction has $\Delta G^\ominus = \pu{+25 kJ mol-1}$ at $\pu{298 K}$. Which best describes its equilibrium mixture at this temperature?
blocks.hint: A positive $\Delta G^\ominus$ means $K < 1$. Does $K < 1$ mean $K = 0$?

options.text: mostly reactants, with a small amount of products
reactants only, with no products at all
mostly products, with a small amount of reactants
equal concentrations of reactants and products

blocks.explain: $\Delta G^\ominus > 0$ gives $K < 1$, so reactants are favoured. $K$ is small but not zero, so some products are always present.

verify.truth: mostly reactants, with a small amount of products

blocks.prompt: A reaction has $\Delta G^\ominus = \pu{-12.0 kJ mol-1}$ at $\pu{310 K}$. Calculate $K$ to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Rearrange to $K = \mathrm{e}^{-\Delta G^\ominus / RT}$, with $\Delta G^\ominus$ in J.
blocks.explain: $\frac{-\Delta G^\ominus}{RT} = \frac{12000}{8.31 \times 310} = 4.658$, so $K = \mathrm{e}^{4.658} \approx 105$. Negative $\Delta G^\ominus$, so $K > 1$, as expected.

blocks.prompt: A mixture of pure reactants starts to react. What happens to $\Delta G$ as the mixture approaches equilibrium?
blocks.hint: Think about the slope of the curve as it nears the minimum.

options.text: It becomes less negative and reaches zero.
It becomes more negative and reaches a minimum.
It stays equal to the standard value throughout.
It becomes positive once equilibrium is reached.

blocks.explain: $\Delta G$ is the slope of the Gibbs energy curve. The slope flattens as the mixture nears the minimum, so $\Delta G$ rises towards zero and is exactly zero at equilibrium.

verify.truth: It becomes less negative and reaches zero.

blocks.text: Divide $\Delta S^\ominus$ (in $\pu{J K-1 mol-1}$) by 1000 before using it with $\Delta H^\ominus$ (in $\pu{kJ mol-1}$). $T$ is always in kelvin.
At constant temperature and pressure, $\Delta G < 0$ means spontaneous, $\Delta G > 0$ non-spontaneous, and $\Delta G = 0$ at equilibrium. Spontaneous says nothing about rate.
$\Delta H < 0$, $\Delta S > 0$: always spontaneous. $\Delta H > 0$, $\Delta S < 0$: never. Same signs: spontaneous above ($+,+$) or below ($-,-$) the crossover $T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$.
$\Delta G = \Delta G^\ominus + RT\ln Q$, and at equilibrium $\Delta G^\ominus = -RT\ln K$ (data booklet, section 1).
$\Delta G^\ominus < 0$: $K > 1$, products favoured. $\Delta G^\ominus > 0$: $K < 1$, reactants favoured but some products still form.

mistakes: Mixing kJ and J. $\Delta S^\ominus$ is given in $\pu{J K-1 mol-1}$, so divide it by 1000 before combining it with $\Delta H^\ominus$.
Using a Celsius temperature in $T\Delta S$ or $RT\ln K$. Convert to kelvin first.
Giving a negative temperature as the crossover. When $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ have opposite signs, there is no crossover temperature at all.
Saying a spontaneous reaction is fast. $\Delta G$ shows whether a change can happen on its own; the rate depends on the activation energy.
Thinking a positive $\Delta G^\ominus$ means no products form. It means $K < 1$, so reactants are favoured but some products are present.
examTips: "Calculate" $\Delta G^\ominus$: write $\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$, substitute with $\Delta S^\ominus$ already in kJ, and give the answer with its sign and $\pu{kJ mol-1}$.
"Determine" the crossover temperature: set $\Delta G^\ominus = 0$, show $T = \frac{\Delta H^\ominus}{\Delta S^\ominus}$ with matching units, and give $T$ in K.
"Explain" spontaneity: state the signs of $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$, compare $T\Delta S$ with $\Delta H$, then conclude with the sign of $\Delta G$, one point per sentence.
In Paper 1A sign questions, picture the straight line $\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$: at low $T$ the $\Delta H$ term decides, at high $T$ the $T\Delta S$ term does.
